feedback: If you drew a labelled box or a made-up sign instead of the standard symbol, replace it with the recognised symbol from the key — a reader can't interpret invented symbols. (Note: the recognised motor symbol is a circle with the letter M inside, so an M in a circle is correct.)
If the motor and buzzer symbols look the same, compare them against the key and redraw until each is unambiguous.
Check your cell: a single cell is one line-pair (long line positive); a battery is several line-pairs.
activities.intendedInsight: Each component has a standard, recognisable symbol; motor and buzzer are easy to confuse and must be told apart, and the cell convention (line-pairs, long line positive) carries meaning.
learnerActions: With each real component in front of you (cell, wire, bulb/lamp, switch, buzzer, motor), draw its recognised symbol while looking at the object.
Deliberately contrast the motor symbol and the buzzer symbol — draw both side by side and note how they differ.
For the cell, draw the long-line/short-line pair and mark which side is positive; distinguish a single cell (one line-pair) from a battery (several line-pairs/cells).
Assemble a shared symbol key pairing each symbol with a photo or the real component and a note of what it does.
activities.title: Draw it with the object in hand, then build a shared symbol key

feedback: If your wires curve to mirror the real circuit's shape, redraw as a straight-line loop keeping exactly the same connections — the diagram shows connections, not positions.
If the loop is left open or a component is missing, the circuit wouldn't work if built — close the loop and add every component.
A diagram that just 'looks neat' isn't the goal; the goal is that the connections are unambiguous.
activities.intendedInsight: A schematic is not a picture of the physical layout: straight wires and a clean closed loop show the connections clearly, and the spatial arrangement does not carry extra meaning.
learnerActions: Set up or look at a real series circuit containing a cell, switch, bulb, buzzer and motor (with only one cell, some components may work weakly or not at all; the task is to record the connections, not to make everything work).
Draw its diagram using straight-line wires arranged as a tidy closed loop (roughly rectangular), with every component drawn in line.
Check that the loop is closed and no component is missing.
Compare a tidy schematic exemplar with a messy/ambiguous attempt and annotate what makes the tidy one readable.
activities.title: Produce a clean schematic from a real circuit

feedback: If your partner built the wrong circuit, trace back to the symbol or connection that misled them and fix it.
If you couldn't build from a partner's diagram, name exactly what was unclear — that is the feedback that makes a diagram communicate.
Judge the diagram by whether the built circuit matches, not by how pretty it looks.
activities.intendedInsight: A good diagram is the one another person can construct the exact circuit from — which is what forces standard symbols, straight wires and a closed loop.
learnerActions: Translate one way: given a real circuit, draw its diagram using recognised symbols.
Translate the other way: given a diagram, assemble the matching real circuit.
Swap diagrams with a partner and build the circuit from THEIR diagram, then check it matches the circuit they intended.
Discuss where a build went wrong and what in the diagram caused it (non-standard symbol, open loop, ambiguous layout).
activities.title: Two-way translation and the 'can someone else build it?' test

feedback: If you said 'it's got a motor, so it turns', trace the loop and check the switch first — a motor only turns in a complete, switched-on loop.
Check the switch symbol: open means the loop or branch it controls is broken.
For the stretch task, remember that in a single series loop breaking any point stops everything — to switch off only the motor, it must be on its own branch; show that branch clearly.
Describe the functional state (what runs), not only the list of parts.
activities.intendedInsight: Whether a component operates depends on the switch state and a complete loop, not just on the component being present in the drawing; and where a component sits on its own switched branch, a switch can control it without stopping the rest.
learnerActions: Given a diagram with a cell, switch, bulb, buzzer and motor, read each symbol and state what it is.
Read the switch symbol (open or closed) and trace the loop to check it is complete.
Say what operates: does the motor turn? does the bulb light? — and justify by the switch state and loop completeness.

Respond to a stretch counterexample: starting from a single series loop, explain why no single switch in that loop can turn off only the motor while the bulb stays lit; then redraw with the motor on its own branch controlled by its own switch (a simple branched arrangement, beyond a single series loop), keeping the bulb on a complete path to the cell, so that opening that switch turns off ONLY the motor while the bulb still lights.
activities.title: Interpret a diagram: read the switch and the loop before deciding what runs
